solutions.check: 30 entries; each light the paper's grid did not give solved here from its clue's wordplay (an anagram or hidden word, the one listed word fitting every crossing) and its definition (WordNet), as the answer another puzzle gave the same clue, or as the one past answer its crossings left that the printed letters allow, agrees with the 29 answers the paper printed

clue.text: Root love out from priest, turning sanctimonious

indicators.note: out from tells us to take the letter for love away from the word for priest

parts.note: a parson is a parish priest
love is zero in tennis scoring, written as the letter O

indicators.note: turning tells us to read the word for sanctimonious backwards

parts.note: pi is crossword shorthand for pious or sanctimonious

explanation.surface: A priest drops love and becomes self-righteous, at the root of the matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out from' removes O from PARSON to leave PARSN; 'turning' makes IP from PI.
explanation.definitionFit: The parsnip is a pale vegetable grown for its edible tapering root.

clue.text: A tree generally admired — not yew, by the sound of it

indicators.note: not tells us to drop a letter from the word for generally admired

parts.note: popular means liked by most people

indicators.note: by the sound of it means the tree name yew stands for the letter it sounds like

parts.note: yew is pronounced like the letter U

explanation.surface: A widely liked tree, but not the yew, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: Yew is itself a tree, so it looks like part of the definition; it only supplies the U taken from POPULAR.
explanation.definitionFit: The poplar is a tall fast-growing tree of the willow family.

clue.text: Gave a second hearing, as did Bruce

explanation.surface: A case heard again, as a Scottish king once did.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert the Bruce, the Scottish king, is said to have watched a spider try and try again, and so tried again himself.
explanation.definitionFit: A court that retried a case heard it again; and Bruce made another attempt after defeat.

clue.text: Set aside one — I will enter into the sport got up by Edward

indicators.note: by places the letter for one beside the name that follows
got up in a down clue means the letters are read upwards, back to front
enter into puts the contracted I will inside the word for sport

parts.note: fun is sport, playful amusement
I will contracts to I'll
I is the Roman numeral for one
Ed is short for Edward

explanation.surface: One person joins in the game that Edward organised and it was cancelled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'enter into' gives F-ILL-UN; 'got up' turns it to NULLIF. Then I and ED follow.
explanation.definitionFit: To nullify a ruling is to cancel or annul it, so it is set aside.

clue.text: Put me in late in the order, nearly last

indicators.note: in the order hints that the letters are to be arranged into another sequence

explanation.surface: A batsman asks to be put in late in the batting order.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests cricket's batting order, but 'order' signals rearranging PUT ME IN LATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Penultimate is next to the final one, so last but one.

clue.text: Witnesses attending trials

parts.note: attending a meeting is being at it
tests are trials

explanation.surface: People giving evidence turn up at court hearings.
explanation.definitionFit: To witness a document is to certify it, a verb sense matching the third-person form.

clue.text: Expert appearing in suit

explanation.surface: A skilled player turns up in a smart outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is the playing card: every suit of cards contains one.
explanation.definitionFit: A champion or virtuoso is an ace; and the top card of each suit in a pack is the ace.

clue.text: Subject to selection, so to speak, when divided

indicators.note: so to speak means the phrase is spoken, and its sound gives the answer

parts.note: to stays as written; selection is a pick

explanation.surface: A matter is put to a vote and opinion is split.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when divided' explains the pun: split as TO PIC, the answer sounds like 'to pick'.
explanation.definitionFit: A topic is a theme for discussion, the matter or subject being talked about.

clue.text: Incentives keep half of us within set limits

indicators.note: within tells us the half word goes inside the rearranged limits
set suggests the letters of limits are set out in a new order
half of takes the first of the two letters of us

explanation.surface: Inducements keep some of us inside agreed boundaries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set' turns LIMITS into STIMLI; 'half of' us gives U, placed 'within' to make STIM-U-LI.
explanation.definitionFit: Stimuli are spurs to action, things that rouse a response, much like encouragements.

clue.text: NCO fell in Hamlet

explanation.surface: A non-commissioned officer collapsed during a Shakespeare play.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet, dying, speaks of 'this fell sergeant, Death'; 'fell' there means cruel, not fallen.
explanation.definitionFit: A sergeant is a non-commissioned army rank; and Hamlet's cruel ('fell') officer is Death the sergeant.

clue.text: Favourite uncle upset about a fit of the sulks

parts.note: a pet is a favourite

indicators.note: about tells us the scrambled uncle goes round the letter A
upset tells us the letters of uncle are knocked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A favourite uncle is put out by someone's bout of sulking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' scrambles the uncle into ULNCE, and 'about' wraps that round the A to give ULANCE. 'Favourite uncle' looks like one person, but the favourite is a separate piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Petulance is peevish ill temper, the mood of someone sulking childishly.

clue.text: Previous head of the community

explanation.surface: The former leader of a religious house.
explanation.definitionFit: Prior means earlier, and is also the title of the superior of a priory of monks.

clue.text: A politician has just one excuse

parts.note: Lib is short for a Liberal politician
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A politician has only one excuse to offer.
explanation.definitionFit: An alibi is a plea of having been elsewhere, so a reason offered to avoid blame.

clue.text: Food is the centre of the globe to a Liverpudlian

indicators.note: the centre of picks out the letters of globe without its first and last

parts.note: Scouse is the nickname for a native of Liverpool and their dialect

explanation.surface: A Liverpool native thinks some food is the centre of the world.
explanation.walkthrough: Lobscouse is a sailors' meat-and-vegetable stew, the dish that gave Liverpudlians the name Scousers.
explanation.definitionFit: Lobscouse is a hash or stew, a kind of dish eaten as a meal.

clue.text: Fearfully limited inspiration

parts.note: breath held back, restrained through anxiety, as in waiting with suspense

explanation.definitionFit: Waiting with held-in breathing means waiting in anxious suspense, gasping only shallowly.

clue.text: Martin's an idiot, working in management

indicators.note: working suggests the letters are worked over into a new arrangement

parts.note: the apostrophe is ignored, keeping the S as a letter
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone claims Martin is a fool at his job in the managing office.
explanation.definitionFit: The running of an organisation, its executive control, is its management.

clue.text: Reptilian kind of pear

explanation.surface: A pear that looks like a reptile.
explanation.walkthrough: The alligator pear is an old name for the avocado, from its rough green skin.
explanation.definitionFit: A large reptile of the crocodile family; and the avocado is called the alligator pear.

clue.text: Is a ringer a yellowish-grey?

parts.note: a bell is something that rings
taken as written

explanation.surface: A question whether a lookalike has a greyish-yellow colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Isabella is an old name for a greyish-yellow or dun colour.

clue.text: Enigmatic composer

parts.note: reads as a mysterious musician, but points to the English composer of the Enigma Variations

explanation.surface: A mysterious writer of music.
explanation.definitionFit: He wrote the Enigma Variations, so he is the composer of the Enigma.

clue.text: Article rewritten for public performance

indicators.note: rewritten suggests the letters of the word article are written out again in another order

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece is revised to be read out to an audience.
explanation.definitionFit: A recital is a concert or reading given before an audience.

clue.text: Unfavourable for Anthony

explanation.surface: Things look bad for a man called Anthony.
explanation.walkthrough: Anthony Adverse is a 1933 best-selling historical novel by Hervey Allen, later a film.
explanation.definitionFit: Adverse means hostile or harmful; and it is the surname of the hero of a famous novel.

clue.text: Believe common 25dn about communist

indicators.note: about tells us the vulgar townsman goes round the communist

parts.note: 25 down is a cad; cit is old slang for a common, vulgar townsman, an ill-bred fellow
a red is a communist

explanation.surface: Trust a vulgar bounder to wrap himself around a communist.
explanation.walkthrough: CIT, short for citizen, was a sneering term for a low-bred city tradesman.
explanation.definitionFit: To credit a story is to accept it as true, to trust it.

clue.text: Dollar, a loan requested by Antony verbally — he was an adventurer

indicators.note: verbally means the phrase is spoken, and its sound gives the letters

parts.words: Dollar, a loan requested by Antony
parts.note: a buck is a dollar; Mark Antony's speech asks 'lend me your ears', so the loan he requests is an ear

explanation.surface: A dollar loaned to Antony belonged to a daring adventurer.
explanation.walkthrough: In Julius Caesar, Antony begins 'Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears', so the thing he asks to borrow is an ear: BUCK, AN EAR said quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: A buccaneer was a pirate of the Caribbean, a reckless seafaring adventurer.

clue.text: Bolt from Cockney school

indicators.note: Cockney speakers famously drop the letter H, so the school's name loses it

parts.note: Harrow is a famous English public school in north-west London

explanation.surface: A runaway escapes from a London school.
explanation.definitionFit: A bolt is a short heavy arrow shot from a crossbow.

clue.text: With king around, I have to be a contributor

indicators.note: around says the king's letters wrap the contracted I have

parts.note: GR is Georgius Rex, King George
I have contracts to I've

explanation.surface: Under the king, I have to give my share.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who gives money or help to a cause is a donor or contributor.

clue.text: After making mischief between two sides

indicators.note: between places the mischief word inside the two side letters

parts.note: L and R are left and right, the two sides
Ate is the Greek goddess of mischief and ruin

explanation.surface: Someone causes trouble between two rival camps afterwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Later means afterwards, subsequently in time.

clue.text: Given a document, a note, burned round the edge

indicators.note: round the edge tells us the burned word encircles the note at its border

parts.note: charred means scorched or burned
te is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A document with a note on it has been singed at the edges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round the edge' sets the note inside the scorched word, splitting it as CHAR and RED either side.
explanation.definitionFit: A chartered body has been granted a charter, a formal deed giving it rights.

clue.text: Unpleasant character featured in Conservative commercial

parts.note: an ad is a commercial or advertisement

explanation.surface: A nasty piece of work appears in a Tory advertisement.
explanation.definitionFit: A cad is a man who behaves dishonourably, a bounder.

clue.text: Let, but nothing paid yet

explanation.surface: Rooms are let out, but no money has come in.
explanation.walkthrough: The stray full stop is a speck on the page. The second definition splits the answer into ALL OWED, every penny still due.
explanation.definitionFit: To let is to permit; and if everything is still owing, nothing has been paid.

clue.text: What farmer ends with, having got own way about it

definitions.text: What farmer ends with, having got own way about it

indicators.note: about it says the pieces for own and way go round the letter just picked

parts.note: to own something is to have it

indicators.note: ends with picks the final letter of farmer

parts.note: St is short for street, a way

explanation.surface: What a farmer gets at the end of the season, after getting his way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ends with' gives R, the final letter of farmer, and 'about it' wraps the own and way pieces round it. Read whole, the clue also describes the crop a farmer gathers at the season's end.
explanation.definitionFit: The gathering of crops is the reward a farmer reaps at the close of the growing year.
